result: Non-centromeric DNA circles accumulate in a subset of mother cells and localize to a single place at the nuclear periphery. After 3 hours of centromere excision, 68% of cells show plasmids away from SPBs as small foci. After 16-18 hours, 93% of cells contain no plasmid while 6% show one large intense signal (8-fold above background), corresponding to accumulated plasmids in aged mother cells (5.2±1.9 bud scars vs 0.7±0.9 in cells without plasmids).
evaluation: Claims C24-C30 provide consistent quantitative data showing asymmetric segregation and accumulation of plasmids in mother cells. The bud scar analysis (C29) confirms these are aged mother cells, and the localization data (C30) shows plasmids collect at the nuclear periphery rather than diffusing freely. The progression from dispersed foci at 3h to accumulated mass at 18h is well-documented.

result: Accumulation of DNA circles causes dramatic changes in nuclear pore complex (NPC) distribution, leading to formation of an NPC cap. Circle-loaded nuclei are 1.7-fold larger and contain 2.7-fold more NPCs (independent of reporter used: Nup82-3sfGFP, Nup82-GFP, Nup49-GFP). All circle-loaded cells exhibit an NPC cap covering the DNA circles, with 2-fold higher NPC fluorescence intensity in the circle vicinity. Time-lapse imaging shows the NPC cap and plasmid patch move together.
evaluation: Claims C31-C36 provide robust quantitative evidence with multiple independent NPC reporters showing consistent effects. The co-movement of NPC cap and plasmids (C36) supports a physical linkage. The data are internally consistent and use appropriate controls (cells without plasmids, multiple reporters).

result: During mitosis, cells with accumulated circles show enhanced asymmetric segregation of both circles and NPCs to the mother cell. Mother cells with accumulated plasmids retain 78% of NPCs compared to 63% in cells without circles (p<0.001). The NPC cap and plasmids localize to the mother side of the nuclear bridge during division, with only 2% of cells showing plasmid transmission to the bud.
evaluation: Claims C37-C41 demonstrate coordinated retention of circles and NPCs during mitosis with clear quantitative data. The localization to the mother side of the nuclear bridge (C40) provides mechanistic insight. The low frequency of plasmid transmission (C41) is consistent with high-fidelity retention.

result: The lateral diffusion barrier partially contributes to circle and NPC cap retention. In bud6Δ cells lacking the diffusion barrier, the NPC cap still forms around plasmids, but 11% of cells transmit plasmids to daughters (vs 2% in wild-type), indicating the barrier is necessary but not sufficient for complete retention.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 show that bud6Δ cells retain NPC cap formation but have increased plasmid transmission, demonstrating the barrier's role while indicating additional mechanisms are required. The quantitative comparison (11% vs 2%) is statistically meaningful and supports the conclusion of partial dependence.

result: The SAGA complex and its acetyltransferase activity are required for efficient DNA circle retention in mother cells. Wild-type cells show low plasmid propagation frequency (pf=3.9±1.1), while gcn5Δ, spt3Δ, and sgf73Δ mutants all show significantly increased propagation (pf=11.1±2.8, 9.7±1.7, and 11.8±1.6 respectively). The catalytically inactive gcn5-E173A mutant shows similar defects (pf=11.0±1.5), demonstrating the acetyltransferase activity is essential.
evaluation: Claims C45-C51 provide consistent genetic evidence across multiple SAGA components and include a critical point mutant control (C50) demonstrating the enzymatic activity is required. The propagation frequencies in SAGA mutants match predictions from the passive diffusion model, supporting loss of active retention. Multiple independent clones were tested (N=3) with appropriate statistics.

result: SAGA mediates retention of endogenous extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) in mother cells. In wild-type cells, 38%±6% retain all ERCs in mothers, reduced 2.5-fold in gcn5Δ and sgf73Δ mutants (16±2% and 15±2%). Aged SAGA mutant cells contain fewer ERCs than wild-type. While sgf73Δ shows 2-fold decreased ERC formation, gcn5Δ shows 1.5-fold increased formation, indicating the slow ERC accumulation in gcn5Δ results from retention failure rather than reduced formation.
evaluation: Claims C52-C57 demonstrate SAGA's role extends to endogenous ERCs using multiple complementary assays (segregation tracking, Southern blot, formation rate). The differential effects on ERC formation between gcn5Δ and sgf73Δ (C55-C56) strengthen the conclusion that retention defects, not formation defects, explain reduced accumulation in gcn5Δ.

result: SAGA does not affect nuclear geometry, anaphase duration, or the diffusion barrier. Deletion of YKU70 prolonged anaphase as expected, but deletion of GCN5 or SGF73 did not (N≥180 cells). Nuclear bridge width was unchanged in gcn5Δ cells (N≥70). FLIP experiments showed bud6Δ reduced envelope compartmentalization as reported, but gcn5Δ had no effect (N≥20 cells), indicating SAGA functions through a different mechanism than these morpho-kinetic parameters.
evaluation: Claims C58-C63 systematically rule out alternative mechanisms using appropriate positive controls (yku70Δ for anaphase, bud6Δ for barrier). The negative results are well-controlled and support the conclusion that SAGA acts through a distinct pathway. Sample sizes are adequate for these measurements.

result: SAGA and the NPC component TREX-2 act together in a non-additive pathway to retain DNA circles. Inactivation of SAC3 (core TREX-2 gene) increased circle propagation 3-fold (pf=11.5±3.0), similar to SAGA mutants. Deletion of SUS1 (inactivating both SAGA and TREX-2) or double deletion of GCN5 and SAC3 showed similar effects (pf=11.3±1.4 and 11.1±1.3), indicating non-additive genetic interaction.
evaluation: Claims C64-C67 use appropriate genetic epistasis analysis to demonstrate SAGA and TREX-2 function in the same pathway. The non-additivity of double mutants (C66) is a strong indicator of pathway interaction. Multiple independent clones were tested with consistent results.

result: SAGA promotes physical interaction of DNA circles with nuclear pores. In wild-type cells, only 15%±2.8% of plasmid foci are at resolvable distance from the nuclear envelope, increasing to 31.9%±1.3% in gcn5Δ and 24.1%±2.6% in sus1Δ mutants. Quantitative analysis shows Nup82-3sfGFP intensity increases 33.2%±0.09% near circles in wild-type but not in gcn5Δ (+4.6%±0.05%) or sus1Δ (-2.0%±0.07%) mutants.
evaluation: Claims C68-C73 provide both qualitative (localization) and quantitative (intensity measurements) evidence for SAGA-dependent circle-NPC interaction. The high-resolution imaging with LED illumination minimizes motion blur. The consistent loss of NPC enrichment near circles in SAGA mutants strongly supports the conclusion.

result: Artificial tethering of circles to stable NPCs bypasses the requirement for SAGA but not the diffusion barrier. Nup170-TetR and Nup49-TetR fusions had no effect in wild-type cells (pf=5.5±0.7 and 4.6±1.6) but restored retention in gcn5Δ, sgf73Δ, and sus1Δ mutants. However, these fusions did not rescue retention in bud6Δ cells (pf=11.9±1.8 and 10.8±1.2), demonstrating both tethering and the barrier are required.
evaluation: Claims C74-C78 use elegant genetic rescue experiments to demonstrate SAGA's primary function is tethering circles to NPCs. The failure to rescue bud6Δ (C77) is critical for establishing that both mechanisms are required. The experimental design with appropriate controls is sound.

result: The stability of nucleoporin association with NPCs correlates with ability to mediate circle retention. FRAP experiments show Nup2, Mlp1, and Nup60 diffuse more rapidly than core nucleoporins Nup1, Nup49, and Nup170 during anaphase. The stable association of nucleoporins with NPCs is highly correlated with their ability to mediate circle retention, indicating SAGA functions through promoting stable anchorage to NPCs.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 provide mechanistic insight by correlating NPC dynamics with retention function. The FRAP data (C79) are quantitative and the correlation analysis (C80) is appropriate. This explains why only certain nucleoporin fusions rescue SAGA mutants, strengthening the overall model.

result: The main function of Sgf73 and Sus1 in plasmid retention is physically linking SAGA to nuclear pores. Gcn5-Sac3 and Spt7-Nup49 fusion proteins had no effect in wild-type cells (pf=5.2±0.4 and 4.1±1.0) but largely bypassed the need for Sgf73 (pf=6.1±1.3 and 6.8±2.0 vs 11.8±1.6 in sgf73Δ) and Sus1 (pf=6.5±1.3 and 5.6±0.2 vs 11.3±1.4 in sus1Δ), demonstrating these proteins function primarily as physical linkers.
evaluation: Claims C82-C86 use synthetic fusion proteins to bypass the normal SAGA-NPC interaction, providing strong evidence for the physical linking function. The rescue is substantial though not complete, which is reasonable given the artificial nature of the fusions. The experimental design is sophisticated and well-controlled.

result: SAGA preferentially associates with non-centromeric DNA circles compared to chromosomal DNA. Microscopy shows Gcn5-GFP and Sgf73-GFP are strongly enriched in plasmid areas. ChIP experiments (N=5) show clear enrichment of Gcn5 and Spt20 on non-centromeric reporter plasmid (pYB1670/CEN-) at ARS and non-coding sequences. This enrichment is nearly lost (p<0.05) when the same plasmid contains a centromere (CEN+).
evaluation: Claims C87-C90 use complementary approaches (microscopy and ChIP) to demonstrate preferential SAGA binding to non-centromeric DNA. The comparison between CEN+ and CEN- versions of the same plasmid (C89) is a critical control. Five independent ChIP experiments provide statistical robustness.

result: Binding of SAGA to circles is required for efficient retention. Expression of Gcn5-TetR fusion protein reduced circle propagation 3-fold compared to wild-type (pf=1.1±0.3, p<0.001), while Sir2-TetR (a deacetylase) caused circles to segregate as frequently as SAGA-defective cells, demonstrating that SAGA binding to circles is necessary for retention.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 use targeted recruitment experiments to demonstrate SAGA binding is functionally important. The Sir2-TetR control (C92) is particularly valuable as it shows that simply tethering any protein is insufficient. The 3-fold improvement with Gcn5-TetR is substantial and statistically significant.

result: SAGA-dependent attachment of circles to pores promotes retention of both circles and NPCs. In contrast to wild-type cells, accumulation of DNA circles had no effect on pore segregation in gcn5Δ and sgf73Δ mutant cells, demonstrating that SAGA-dependent attachment promotes retention of the attached NPCs as well as the circles.
evaluation: Claims C94-C95 demonstrate reciprocal effects of the SAGA-mediated interaction. The loss of enhanced NPC retention in SAGA mutants despite circle accumulation is strong evidence that the physical linkage affects both components. This is consistent with the model and well-controlled.

result: SAGA-dependent attachment of DNA circles substantially reduces NPC mobility. FLIP experiments in wild-type cells show NPC signal decays slower near circles (t70=82±39s) than opposite side (t70=25±8s, N=20, p<0.001). In SAGA-deficient cells, circles don't cluster and no NPC cap forms, with uniform NPC distribution. This establishes that in circle-free cells, few NPCs are stably attached to chromatin, while circle-bound NPCs show very slow dynamics, possibly explaining their enhanced retention during mitosis.
evaluation: Claims C96-C101 use FLIP to demonstrate reduced NPC mobility near circles in a SAGA-dependent manner. The quantitative measurements (C96) are robust with appropriate statistics. The inability to perform the same experiment in SAGA mutants due to lack of clustering (C97) is a limitation but the uniform distribution serves as an important control. The speculation about retention mechanism (C101) is appropriately qualified.

result: Non-chromosomal DNA circles and NPCs reciprocally constrain each other's diffusion speed in a SAGA-dependent manner. Time-lapse microscopy shows DNA circles move significantly faster in gcn5Δ cells (0.09±0.027 μm/s) than in wild-type (0.05±0.019 μm/s, N≥50 plasmids, p<0.001), demonstrating mutual constraint of diffusion.
evaluation: Claims C102-C103 provide direct measurements of circle mobility showing SAGA-dependent constraint. The sample size (N≥50 plasmids) is adequate and the statistical significance is clear. This complements the NPC mobility data and supports the model of physical linkage affecting both components.

result: Asymmetric NPC segregation increases with cellular age, leading to NPC accumulation in old mother cells. A large majority of aged cells show non-uniform NPC distribution with cap formation. For all three NPC markers (Nup49, Nup170, Nup82), fluorescence intensity increases significantly in mother nuclei with age. Young mothers retain 56-57% of NPCs, increasing to 73-78% after 25-35 generations.
evaluation: Claims C104-C110 use microfluidic aging to track NPC segregation over time with multiple independent reporters. The progressive increase in asymmetry is well-documented with appropriate quantification. The consistency across three different NPC markers strengthens the conclusions. The microfluidic approach allows tracking of individual cells over their lifespan.

result: Old mother cells accumulate NPCs in a diffusion barrier-dependent manner. Old mothers contain 4.0-4.7-fold more NPCs than young cells after 25-35 generations. Old nuclei are both larger (radius 1.5-fold) and more densely populated with pores (1.9-fold increase in density). The increase in NPC asymmetry, retention, and number is much slower in bud6Δ cells lacking the diffusion barrier.
evaluation: Claims C111-C114 quantify age-dependent NPC accumulation and demonstrate barrier dependence. The measurements of both nuclear size and NPC density (C112) show the effect is not simply due to nuclear growth. The bud6Δ control (C113) demonstrates the diffusion barrier is required for age-dependent accumulation.

result: ERC accumulation drives NPC retention in aging cells. NPC retention and total pores in G1 cells increase much slower with age in fob1Δ mutant cells (reduced ERC formation) and faster in sir2Δ mutant cells (increased ERC formation) compared to wild-type, irrespective of reporter used (Nup49-GFP or Nup170-GFP).
evaluation: Claims C115-C117 use genetic manipulation of ERC levels to demonstrate causality. The opposite effects of fob1Δ and sir2Δ on NPC accumulation rate provide strong evidence that ERCs drive the phenotype. Multiple NPC reporters show consistent results.

result: SAGA mediates the interaction of ERCs and NPCs during aging, leading to their joint retention and accumulation. sgf73Δ mutant cells accumulate NPCs slowly as they age. Artificially linking SAGA to NPCs using Gcn5-Sac3 and Spt7-Nup49 fusion proteins restores NPC accumulation in aging sgf73Δ mutant cells.
evaluation: Claims C118-C120 connect the SAGA-dependent mechanism to endogenous aging. The slow NPC accumulation in sgf73Δ (C118) and rescue by SAGA-NPC fusion proteins (C119) demonstrate the mechanism operates during natural aging with ERCs. This bridges the reporter plasmid and endogenous ERC systems.

result: Different SAGA components have distinct effects on lifespan. sgf73Δ cells live 60% longer than wild-type (44 vs 27 generations, N=150, p<0.001), while gcn5Δ and spt20Δ show no increased longevity (27 and 17 generations). Removing Fob1 fails to extend lifespan of gcn5Δ or spt20Δ mutants, indicating these cells age through mechanisms independent of ERC formation and accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C121-C126 show complex genetic interactions with lifespan. The differential effects of SAGA component deletions are well-documented with adequate sample sizes. The epistasis analysis with fob1Δ (C124-C125) supports the conclusion that gcn5Δ and spt20Δ have ERC-independent aging defects. However, the interpretation is complex as SAGA has multiple functions.

result: Decreased SAGA levels at pores contribute to extended lifespan in sgf73Δ cells. Gcn5-Sac3 and Spt7-Nup49 fusion proteins don't alter wild-type longevity (27 generations) but substantially shorten sgf73Δ lifespan (16 and 34 generations vs 44 in sgf73Δ, N≥50, p<0.01), demonstrating that reduced SAGA at pores contributes to the longevity phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C127-C130 use the SAGA-NPC fusion proteins to demonstrate that restoring SAGA function at pores reverses the longevity benefit of sgf73Δ. This is strong evidence that the longevity effect is specifically due to reduced SAGA-NPC interaction. The experimental design is sophisticated and well-controlled.

result: SAGA promotes aging through promoting anchorage of non-chromosomal DNA circles to NPCs and their joint retention and accumulation with age. Non-chromosomal DNA circles alone do not accumulate and do not promote aging if they are not at NPCs.
evaluation: Claims C131-C132 represent the main conclusions integrating all the experimental evidence. The data from plasmid retention, ERC accumulation, NPC dynamics, aging experiments, and genetic rescue all support this model. The conclusion that circles must be at NPCs to promote aging is well-supported by the sgf73Δ longevity and the failure of gcn5Δ fob1Δ to extend lifespan.

result: A unifying model proposes that both morpho-kinetic parameters and tethering to NPCs are required for efficient circle retention, with the diffusion barrier efficiently retaining circle-bound NPCs rather than NPCs or circles alone. This model integrates the morpho-kinetic baseline retention with SAGA-mediated tethering for high-fidelity retention.
evaluation: Claims C133-C135 present a synthesis model that reconciles previous conflicting models. The data showing SAGA mutants have retention frequencies matching passive diffusion predictions (C48-C49), the requirement for both tethering and barrier (C77), and the enhanced retention of circle-bound NPCs (C39, C95) all support this integrated model. This is appropriately presented as a proposed model in the Discussion.

result: Background on DNA circle formation and effects in eukaryotes. Intra-chromosomal recombination generates DNA circles in eukaryotes, with 50% of events leading to circle excision. rDNA circles are found in all eukaryotes tested. In S. cerevisiae, ERCs form spontaneously, replicate in S-phase, segregate asymmetrically, and accumulate in mother cells. Mutations affecting ERC formation or retention alter lifespan, and any replicating circle lacking a centromere segregates asymmetrically and promotes aging.
evaluation: Claims C1-C18 provide established background knowledge with appropriate citations. These are well-accepted facts in the field and provide necessary context for the study. The claims are properly attributed to prior work.

result: Two existing models for circle retention: the morpho-kinetic model proposes circles freely diffuse with retention resulting from nuclear geometry and short anaphase (predicting retention frequency 0.75-0.90), while mathematical modeling indicates observed aging requires retention >0.99. The barrier model proposes circles attach to nuclear envelope receptors for confinement by the lateral diffusion barrier.
evaluation: Claims C19-C23 accurately describe prior models with appropriate citations. The discrepancy between morpho-kinetic predictions (C20) and mathematical modeling requirements (C21) sets up the rationale for the current study. These are well-established prior findings.
